```{r setup, include=FALSE}
## ── ONE SWITCH (set in the YAML header) ──────────────────────────────────────
##   params$recompute = FALSE : load pre-computed results from lr_demo_data/  (fast; default)
##                    = TRUE  : re-run lppls_rolling() / lr_trend_test() and refresh lr_demo_data/
## The expensive chunks are gated `eval = RECOMPUTE`; a hidden loader (gated
## `eval = !RECOMPUTE`) reads the cached objects back under the SAME names, so every
## display chunk below is identical in both modes and the knitted output matches.
RECOMPUTE <- isTRUE(params$recompute)
B_BOOT    <- params$B_boot
D         <- "lr_demo_data"

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 110)

## Locate and load the package from source, wherever this file is knit from.
pkg_root <- "."
for (up in c(".", "..", file.path("..", ".."), file.path("..", "..", ".."))) {
  if (file.exists(file.path(up, "DESCRIPTION"))) { pkg_root <- up; break }
}
suppressMessages(pkgload::load_all(pkg_root, quiet = TRUE))
suppressMessages(library(ggplot2))

## The heavy Suggests are needed ONLY to recompute lr_trend_test(); the vignette
## (recompute = FALSE) renders without them.
if (RECOMPUTE) suppressMessages({
  library(parallel); library(sandwich); library(tsgarch); library(xts)
})
n_cores <- if (RECOMPUTE) max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 2L) else 1L
```

This document demonstrates the rolling-window / Lagrange-regularization toolchain
in **`lpplsF`** end to end:

| Step | Function(s) |
|---|---|
| 1. Roll the LPPLS calibration over the start time $T_1$ | `lppls_rolling()` |
| 2. Inspect the window estimates | `rolling_tc_plot()`, `rolling_param_plot()` |
| 3. Pick the optimal window by Lagrange regularization | `lppls_lagrange()`, `chi_sq_np_plot()`, `chi_sq_lambda_plot()` |
| 4. Ask whether the regularized trend is *real* or a noise artifact | `lr_trend_test()` |

The idea behind Lagrange regularization (Demos & Sornette, 2019) is that a
genuine bubble has a well-defined beginning: as the calibration start $T_1$
sweeps forward, the normalized fit residual $\chi^2_{np}(T_1)$ should *fall*
once the window is dominated by the log-periodic signal. Regularization removes
the mechanical "more data ⇒ larger residual" trend and reports the window
$T_1^*$ that best balances fit against sample size. `lr_trend_test()` then asks
the harder question — is that downward trend distinguishable from what pure
estimation noise produces on its own?

> **Reproducibility.** The expensive fitting is cached under `lr_demo_data/`. Knit as-is
> (`recompute = FALSE`) to reload it (seconds); knit with
> `rmarkdown::render("lr_demo.Rmd", params = list(recompute = TRUE))` to re-run
> everything (a few minutes, and it needs the suggested packages `tsgarch`,
> `xts`, `sandwich`, `parallel`).

# Two synthetic series

We build two log-price series that a rolling calibration should treat very
differently. Both are 500 points long with the same Gaussian noise realization
($\sigma = 0.05$); the only difference is the presence of a regime change.

* **Regime switch** — a flat "ranging" market for the first `onset = 250`
  observations that then switches into an LPPLS bubble. There is a genuine start
  date to find.
* **Single regime** — a pure LPPLS bubble the whole way through. There is no
  special start date; the log-periodic signal is present from $t = 1$.

```{r data}
set.seed(3630)
N <- 500; onset <- 250; sigma <- 0.05

## The underlying LPPLS bubble (critical time just past the sample end)
bubble <- eval_lppls(seq_len(N), A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
                     tc = N + 1, m = 0.6, omega = 8)

## Regime switch: flat prefix at the onset level, then the bubble
set.seed(3630)
lp_regime <- c(rep(bubble[onset], onset), bubble[(onset + 1):N]) + rnorm(N) * sigma

## Single regime: the bubble throughout (same noise draw)
set.seed(3630)
lp_single <- bubble + rnorm(N) * sigma
```

```{r plot-data, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.2}
df <- rbind(
  data.frame(t = seq_len(N), logp = lp_regime, series = "regime switch (flat -> LPPLS)"),
  data.frame(t = seq_len(N), logp = lp_single, series = "single regime (LPPLS + noise)")
)
ggplot(df, aes(t, logp)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = onset, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~series) +
  labs(x = "time index", y = "log price") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The dashed line marks the true onset (`t = 250`). We walk through the toolchain
on the **regime-switch** series, then use both series to contrast `lr_trend_test()`.

# Rolling-window calibration — `lppls_rolling()`

`lppls_rolling()` is the expensive primitive: it calibrates one LPPLS model per
window, all sharing a common calibration end $T_2$ while the start $T_1$
rolls over `t1_seq`. The last `hold_out` points are reserved from the end, which
fixes $T_2$. We roll in `mode = "MPL"` so the modified-profile-likelihood
intervals for $t_c$ are captured too.

```{r roll-config}
t1_seq   <- seq(1, 250, by = 30)          # 9 rolling start times
fit_args <- list(lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.03, 0.8),
                 upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
                 m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12,
                 num_searches = 1, mode = "MPL")
```

```{r compute-roll, eval=RECOMPUTE}
roll_regime <- lppls_rolling(lp_regime, t1_seq = t1_seq, hold_out = 50, fh = 18,
                             fit_args = fit_args)
roll_single <- lppls_rolling(lp_single, t1_seq = t1_seq, hold_out = 50, fh = 18,
                             fit_args = fit_args)
```

```{r save-roll, eval=RECOMPUTE, echo=FALSE}
dir.create(D, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(roll_regime, file.path(D, "roll_regime.rds"))
saveRDS(roll_single, file.path(D, "roll_single.rds"))
```

```{r load-roll, eval=!RECOMPUTE, echo=FALSE}
roll_regime <- readRDS(file.path(D, "roll_regime.rds"))
roll_single <- readRDS(file.path(D, "roll_single.rds"))
```

The returned object prints a compact summary:

```{r roll-print}
roll_regime
```

`rolling_tc_plot()` shows the $t_c$ point estimate (profile likelihood in black,
modified profile likelihood in cyan) with its 5 % / 10 % / 50 % likelihood-interval
bands, as a function of $T_1$. As the window starts to include the post-onset
bubble, the critical-time estimate settles down:

```{r roll-tc, fig.height=4.2}
rolling_tc_plot(roll_regime)
```

`rolling_param_plot()` shows the six LPPLS parameters
$(m, \omega, A, B, C_1, C_2)$ across the same windows:

```{r roll-param, fig.height=6}
rolling_param_plot(roll_regime)
```

# Lagrange regularization — `lppls_lagrange()`

`lppls_lagrange()` is cheap post-processing on the rolling object: it normalizes
each window's residual sum of squares to $\chi^2_{np}(T_1)$, fits the linear
bias trend $\chi^2_{np} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_1$, and reports the regularized
minimizer $T_1^*$. We use `p = 0`, the "p-correction omitted" form of Demos &
Sornette (2019).

```{r lagrange}
lag_regime <- lppls_lagrange(roll_regime, p = 0)
lag_regime
```

`chi_sq_np_plot()` shows $\chi^2_{np}(T_1)$ with the fitted bias trend (red).
A genuine bubble onset produces a downward slope — $\lambda^* = -\beta_1 > 0$:

```{r lag-np, fig.height=4}
chi_sq_np_plot(lag_regime)
```

`chi_sq_lambda_plot()` shows the regularized objective
$\chi^2_{\lambda^*}(T_1) = \chi^2_{np}(T_1) - \lambda^*(T_2 - T_1)$, with a
green line at the optimal start $T_1^*$:

```{r lag-lambda, fig.height=4}
chi_sq_lambda_plot(lag_regime)
```

# Is the trend real? — `lr_trend_test()`

A downward $\chi^2_{np}$ slope is only meaningful if it is larger than what
estimation noise alone would generate. This is subtle because adjacent rolling
windows overlap heavily, so $\chi^2_{np}(T_1)$ is strongly autocorrelated and a
naive ordinary-least-squares $p$-value is badly oversized. `lr_trend_test()`
reports three tests:

* **OLS** $p$ — the naive test (invalid here; shown for reference);
* **HAC** $p$ — Newey–West, heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent;
* **parametric AR(1)–GARCH(1,1) bootstrap** $p$ — the appropriate test. It fits
  an AR(1)–GARCH(1,1) model to the residuals of the full-window fit, simulates
  fresh noise paths on top of that single fitted LPPLS curve, re-rolls the whole
  calibration on each, and builds the null distribution of $\beta_1$. A validity
  guard flags an IGARCH fit ($\alpha + \beta \ge 1$): if the noise model is
  misspecified the bootstrap is skipped and its $p$-value is `NA`.

We run it on **both** series (the bootstrap re-rolls `B` times, so this is the
expensive step):

```{r compute-lr, eval=RECOMPUTE}
lr_regime <- lr_trend_test(roll_regime, log_price = lp_regime,
                           B = B_BOOT, cores = n_cores, seed = 1)
lr_single <- lr_trend_test(roll_single, log_price = lp_single,
                           B = B_BOOT, cores = n_cores, seed = 1)
```

```{r save-lr, eval=RECOMPUTE, echo=FALSE}
saveRDS(lr_regime, file.path(D, "lr_regime.rds"))
saveRDS(lr_single, file.path(D, "lr_single.rds"))
```

```{r load-lr, eval=!RECOMPUTE, echo=FALSE}
lr_regime <- readRDS(file.path(D, "lr_regime.rds"))
lr_single <- readRDS(file.path(D, "lr_single.rds"))
```

**Regime switch** — a genuine onset:

```{r lr-regime}
lr_regime
```

**Single regime** — a bubble but no special start date:

```{r lr-single}
lr_single
```

Side by side:

```{r lr-table, echo=FALSE}
mk_row <- function(lr, name) {
  data.frame(
    Series        = name,
    `lambda*`     = signif(lr$lambda, 3),
    `OLS p`       = signif(lr$p_ols, 3),
    `HAC p`       = signif(lr$p_hac, 3),
    `Bootstrap p` = signif(lr$p_boot, 3),
    `alpha+beta`  = signif(lr$persist, 3),
    check.names   = FALSE
  )
}
knitr::kable(
  rbind(mk_row(lr_regime, "regime switch"),
        mk_row(lr_single, "single regime")),
  caption = "Three tests of the chi-squared_np bias trend for each series."
)
```

The bootstrap null distribution of the slope $\beta_1$, with the observed slope
in red. For the regime switch the observed slope sits far out in the tail
(significant); for the single regime it sits inside the bulk (a noise artifact):

```{r lr-hist, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.6}
hn <- rbind(
  data.frame(beta1 = lr_regime$null, series = "regime switch"),
  data.frame(beta1 = lr_single$null, series = "single regime")
)
obs <- data.frame(series = c("regime switch", "single regime"),
                  beta1  = c(lr_regime$beta1, lr_single$beta1))
ggplot(hn, aes(beta1)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "grey70", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(data = obs, aes(xintercept = beta1), colour = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~series, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = expression(beta[1]~"(null distribution; red = observed)"), y = "count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Reading the result

The naive **OLS** $p$-value and even the **HAC** $p$-value declare the trend
"significant" for *both* series — including the single-regime series, where by
construction there is nothing to find. They are fooled by the autocorrelation of
overlapping windows. Only the **parametric bootstrap** separates the two cases:
it confirms the trend for the genuine regime switch and correctly reports the
single-regime slope as indistinguishable from noise.

This is the whole point of `lr_trend_test()`: a decreasing $\chi^2_{np}$ trend —
and hence a confident-looking $T_1^*$ from `lppls_lagrange()` — is not by itself
evidence of a datable bubble onset. For a systematic treatment (Monte-Carlo
fragility of $\lambda^*$, onset localization, and the S&P 500 example) see
`misc/lr_exploration/lagrange_inference_report.Rmd`.

> The bootstrap uses only `r params$B_boot` replicates here (kept small for the
> demo); a publication-grade test would use several hundred to a few thousand,
> with `cores > 1` to parallelize the re-rolls.

```{r session, echo=FALSE}
sessionInfo()
```
